quiz.question: You are choosing between a huge partitioned table with a global unique constraint vs uniqueness in the application. PostgreSQL unique indexes are per partition (unless you include the partition key). What is the real design constraint?
quiz.optionA: Global uniqueness is free if you use logical replication.
quiz.optionB: A unique index can only guarantee uniqueness within the index's scope; cross-partition uniqueness needs the partition key in the constraint or an external allocator.
quiz.optionC: Partitioning always preserves all unique constraints of the parent with no extra columns.
quiz.optionD: Unique constraints are enforced by WAL, which is global.

quiz.question: A multi-tenant SaaS puts all tenants in one cluster. One tenant runs analytical queries that blow up work_mem and temp files. What isolation strategy actually protects neighbors?
quiz.optionA: A single `statement_timeout` equal for everyone is enough.
quiz.optionB: Separate roles/pools with memory/timeouts, plus (if needed) separate databases or clusters; Postgres does not give hard multi-tenant CPU isolation inside one instance.
quiz.optionC: MVCC isolates CPU as well as row versions.
quiz.optionD: Put the noisy tenant on a replica and they cannot affect the primary's CPU.

quiz.question: Synchronous replication to a standby in another AZ: commits now wait on the network. A failover-happy load balancer flaps the standby. What failure did you couple into the write path?
quiz.optionA: None; sync replica loss is ignored until you promote.
quiz.optionB: Commits stall or fail when the sync standby is unhealthy; you bought durability/availability of the standby into every write's latency SLO.
quiz.optionC: PostgreSQL automatically falls back to local commits with the same RPO.
quiz.optionD: The primary buffers sync commits in shared buffers indefinitely.

quiz.question: You need close-to-zero downtime DDL on a 10 TB table (add a column with a non-constant default, historically). What is the staff-level instinct?
quiz.optionA: Run it in a transaction on the primary during peak; MVCC makes it instant.
quiz.optionB: Treat it as an expand/contract migration: add nullable column, backfill in batches, then constrain — not one blocking rewrite if the version still rewrites.
quiz.optionC: Logical replication ignores table rewrites, so just ALTER.
quiz.optionD: Global indexes make any DDL O(1).

quiz.question: Connection poolers (PgBouncer) in transaction pooling hide session state. Which app pattern silently breaks?
quiz.optionA: Simple prepared statements that last one transaction.
quiz.optionB: Session-level features: SET, temp tables, WITH HOLD cursors, advisory locks you expected to last the HTTP connection.
quiz.optionC: Read-only queries.
quiz.optionD: Using a single user role.

quiz.question: Group Replication / InnoDB Cluster vs a classic async replica + orchestrated failover. You need to write in two regions. What is the honest limitation?
quiz.optionA: Group Replication gives you active-active multi-region writes with no conflict rules.
quiz.optionB: Multi-primary across high-latency regions is conflict- and latency-hostile; most healthy designs keep a single write primary and regional readers.
quiz.optionC: Async replication cannot be used for reads.
quiz.optionD: GTIDs make two-region writes linearizable.

quiz.question: A huge InnoDB table must be resharded because the PK is a hot increment and one instance is CPU-bound. What is the scaling move that actually works?
quiz.optionA: Add more replicas and send writes to all of them.
quiz.optionB: Split write keyspace across instances (application sharding or a proxy), because one clustered B-tree will not horizontally absorb write CPU.
quiz.optionC: Enable the query cache.
quiz.optionD: Move the table to MEMORY engine.

quiz.question: You observe replication lag that grows only when the primary does bulk LOAD. Row-based replication is on. Why can the replica still fall over?
quiz.optionA: Row-based events for huge writes apply row-by-row on the replica, often without the primary's bulk optimizations.
quiz.optionB: Replicas ignore LOAD DATA.
quiz.optionC: Binlog compresses bulk loads to one page the replica cannot unpack.
quiz.optionD: The replica must take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on every table.

quiz.question: A finance ledger requires 'read your writes' and audit of who changed a row. Why is a read replica the wrong place for the audit query immediately after commit?
quiz.optionA: Replicas have stronger isolation than the primary.
quiz.optionB: Async apply means the replica may not have the row; the audit source of truth is the primary (or a commit-wait / session-consistent mechanism).
quiz.optionC: Binlog does not contain UPDATEs.
quiz.optionD: Audit must be done in the application memory only.

quiz.question: You are picking a storage engine for a write-heavy metrics store with occasional large range scans for graphs. What is the real tension?
quiz.optionA: LSM ingest vs the merge cost of those range scans (and compaction stealing I/O from queries).
quiz.optionB: B-trees cannot store timestamps.
quiz.optionC: LSMs cannot expire old data.
quiz.optionD: Range scans are always O(1) on both.

quiz.question: A team wants 'just put RocksDB in front of S3' as a global database. What staff-level objection is first?
quiz.optionA: RocksDB cannot persist to disk.
quiz.optionB: A local LSM is not a distributed consensus/replication layer; you still need sharding, fencing, and a commit protocol or you will split-brain.
quiz.optionC: S3 cannot store SSTables.
quiz.optionD: Bloom filters do not work outside process memory.

quiz.question: Tombstones in an LSM outlive the data they delete under a bad compaction policy. How do reads fail?
quiz.optionA: They don't; tombstones are skipped in O(1).
quiz.optionB: Point and especially range reads must sift dead keys until compaction drops them; space and CPU inflate.
quiz.optionC: Tombstones automatically promote to the memtable as live keys.
quiz.optionD: The WAL refuses new writes until tombstones are gone.

quiz.question: A globally distributed Cassandra app uses LOCAL_QUORUM in each DC and never repairs. What consistency story are you actually giving users who travel between DCs?
quiz.optionA: Linearizable global reads.
quiz.optionB: A DC-local quorum that can remain stale vs another DC until repair/hint/read-repair; design for it or use a different consistency/replication model.
quiz.optionC: LOCAL_QUORUM waits for all DCs.
quiz.optionD: Hinted handoff makes DCs interchangeable immediately.

quiz.question: You need a uniqueness constraint ('this email is registered') in Cassandra. Why is that a product smell at staff level?
quiz.optionA: Cassandra unique indexes are serializable by default.
quiz.optionB: Uniqueness is a consensus problem; LWT per email works at modest QPS and becomes a hotspot/latency tax. Often the source of truth belongs in a database that does this cheaply.
quiz.optionC: A secondary index on email is unique automatically.
quiz.optionD: Partitioning on email hashes uniqueness for free.

quiz.question: Compaction strategy: STCS on a time-series table that mostly appends and TTLs. Why might TWCS be the better fit?
quiz.optionA: STCS is illegal on time-series.
quiz.optionB: Time-window compaction can drop whole SSTables when TTL expires instead of mixing old/new in size-tiered compaction, reducing tombstone pain.
quiz.optionC: TWCS makes all reads QUORUM.
quiz.optionD: TWCS stores data in B-trees.

quiz.question: A product wants relational joins across three DynamoDB tables on the request path. What should you push back with?
quiz.optionA: Use Scan + in-memory join; DynamoDB is fine.
quiz.optionB: Access-pattern-first: denormalize/duplicate, or pick a database that joins. Request-path joins are N queries, inconsistent snapshots, and hot GSIs waiting to happen.
quiz.optionC: Transactions across three tables are free if items are small.
quiz.optionD: PartiQL joins are as cheap as Dynamo Query.

quiz.question: You are designing for a 10× Prime-Day-like spike on a few product keys. Adaptive capacity and on-demand help, but what still requires modeling work?
quiz.optionA: Nothing; on-demand removes hot keys.
quiz.optionB: A single partition key still has a ceiling; cache, shard the key, or isolate those items so one product cannot concentrate all writes.
quiz.optionC: Global tables spread one key's writes evenly across partitions.
quiz.optionD: DAX makes writes infinitely scalable.

quiz.question: Streams + Lambda to maintain a projection. The Lambda is not idempotent. What operational failure is guaranteed eventually?
quiz.optionA: Streams are exactly-once, so the projection stays correct.
quiz.optionB: At-least-once shard records will double-apply; the projection must be idempotent or versioned.
quiz.optionC: Lambda retries are disabled for DynamoDB streams.
quiz.optionD: Projections cannot diverge because they share storage with the table.

quiz.question: A platform team offers Redis as 'multi-tenant durable storage' with one cluster and no key namespaces/limits. What will happen?
quiz.optionA: Redis ACLs make noisy neighbors impossible.
quiz.optionB: One tenant's large keys, KEYS, or unbounded growth will stall or evict everyone; you need isolation (instances), maxmemory policies, and key prefixes with hard quotas.
quiz.optionC: Cluster slots isolate tenants automatically.
quiz.optionD: AOF rewrite is per key, so tenants cannot interact.

quiz.question: You need a distributed lock. Someone uses SET NX without expiry, or with expiry but no fencing token. What bug remains?
quiz.optionA: None; NX is a correct lock.
quiz.optionB: A lock can be held forever, or expire while work continues and a second worker runs — without fencing, both sides mutate the resource.
quiz.optionC: Redis locks are linearizable if you use WAIT.
quiz.optionD: Expiry is unnecessary if clients are in the same VPC.

quiz.question: Redis is used as a session store. A replica is promoted after async replication lag. What did users just lose, and what is the staff fix?
quiz.optionA: Nothing; promotion waits for replicas.
quiz.optionB: Recent sessions/writes that never made the replica; either accept RPO, use WAIT/sync replication (latency), or don't put irreplaceable sessions only in Redis.
quiz.optionC: AOF on the new primary contains the old primary's unsent writes automatically.
quiz.optionD: Clients reconnect and Redis heals sessions from S3.

quiz.question: A data lake is 'S3 + many writers renaming prefixes to commit'. Why do staff engineers push for a real table format / manifest?
quiz.optionA: Rename is atomic across prefixes in S3 like a filesystem mv of a directory.
quiz.optionB: There is no atomic directory rename; readers can see partial sets. Table formats (or a commit inventory) give a consistent snapshot of files.
quiz.optionC: S3 LIST is a transaction log.
quiz.optionD: Prefix rename is cheaper than writing a manifest.

quiz.question: Cross-account S3 access: bucket policy vs IAM identity policy vs ACL vs VPC endpoint policy. A request is denied. How do you reason?
quiz.optionA: Any one allow wins.
quiz.optionB: All relevant layers must allow and none deny; missing identity permission or a VPC endpoint policy deny will fail the call even if the bucket policy allows.
quiz.optionC: ACLs override IAM.
quiz.optionD: Bucket owner always can, regardless of endpoint policies.

quiz.question: You are asked to put a POSIX-ish shared scratch filesystem on S3 for a database's data directory. What is the right answer?
quiz.optionA: S3 is strongly consistent now, so fsync semantics are met.
quiz.optionB: S3 is an object store, not POSIX: no byte-range locking, no real fsync of a mutable file. Use block storage or a real shared FS designed for that DB.
quiz.optionC: Mountpoint for S3 is equivalent to ext4 for InnoDB.
quiz.optionD: If you enable versioning, POSIX appends work.

quiz.question: etcd is at 8 GB and already slow. Controllers re-list huge objects. What is the cluster-level failure mode?
quiz.optionA: kubelets skip etcd and talk to the graph driver.
quiz.optionB: API latency rises, watches fall behind, heartbeats/elections suffer — the control plane is a strongly consistent store with a size/QPS budget.
quiz.optionC: etcd automatically shards by namespace.
quiz.optionD: This only affects helm, not scheduling.

quiz.question: A multi-tenant cluster lets teams set their own nodeSelectors to dedicated hardware. One team omits requests. What is the platform failure?
quiz.optionA: NodeSelectors replace the need for requests.
quiz.optionB: Without mandatory requests/limits (admission), BestEffort pods still pack onto those nodes and evict or starve the paying workload. Policy must be enforced, not documented.
quiz.optionC: taints prevent BestEffort automatically.
quiz.optionD: QoS is per-namespace and defaults to Guaranteed.

quiz.question: You need zonal disruption (one AZ down) to leave the service up. PDB minAvailable=80% and 3 replicas. Why is that a false SLO?
quiz.optionA: PDBs control node drains, not replica count.
quiz.optionB: 3 replicas cannot lose a zone and still keep 80% (you'd have 2/3). The PDB and topology spread must match the actual failure domain math.
quiz.optionC: Kubernetes will create extra pods when an AZ dies if a PDB exists.
quiz.optionD: minAvailable is of nodes, not pods.

quiz.question: A latency SLO is missed only during old-gen collections on a huge heap. What is the architectural move, not a GC flag trivia answer?
quiz.optionA: Always `-XX:+UseSerialGC` on 256 GB heaps.
quiz.optionB: Shrink live set (off-heap caches, smaller heaps, more instances), or pick a collector/heap size that meets pause goals — GC flags cannot fix a 100 GB live set you treat as a cache.
quiz.optionC: Disable GC and use malloc.
quiz.optionD: One JVM per company is more efficient.

quiz.question: False sharing: two threads update adjacent counters in an array and scale poorly. What is actually happening?
quiz.optionA: The JVM inserts a global lock on int[].
quiz.optionB: They bounce the same cache line between cores; padding/striping (or LongAdder-style cells) separates the lines.
quiz.optionC: int[] is always on-heap so atomics cannot work.
quiz.optionD: This only happens on 32-bit JVMs.

quiz.question: A library registers a JVM shutdown hook that talks to the network. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and kills after terminationGracePeriod. Why is the hook a bad place for flush?
quiz.optionA: Shutdown hooks always get 10 minutes.
quiz.optionB: Hooks race the SIGTERM budget and other hooks; flush in the application lifecycle (Spring close, preStop) with an explicit timeout smaller than the grace period.
quiz.optionC: SIGTERM cannot interrupt Java.
quiz.optionD: Kubernetes never sends SIGKILL.

quiz.question: You inherited a monolith Boot app that starts a full context for every integration test. CI is 40 minutes. What is the staff testing strategy?
quiz.optionA: Only @SpringBootTest; slicing hides bugs.
quiz.optionB: Slice tests for web/data, testcontainers for a few contract tests, and a small number of full-context smoke tests — not a full boot per method.
quiz.optionC: Disable tests in CI to restore speed.
quiz.optionD: Replace JUnit with main() methods.

quiz.question: A payment service must not lose 'charge then record' if the process dies after HTTP 200 from Stripe. What Spring-centric pattern actually works?
quiz.optionA: @Transactional around the Stripe SDK call.
quiz.optionB: Idempotency key + outbox (record intent, commit, then charge/publish) so crash recovery can finish the work without double-charge.
quiz.optionC: @Async so the charge happens after response.
quiz.optionD: XA with Stripe's JDBC driver.

quiz.question: Two Boot services share a database and Hibernate entities. Why do staff platform teams fight this?
quiz.optionA: Hibernate cannot map the same table twice in the world.
quiz.optionB: You coupled deployability and schemas: migrations, locks, and incompatible entity changes become a distributed monolith. Split data ownership.
quiz.optionC: Spring forbids two apps on one JDBC URL.
quiz.optionD: Connection pools cannot be sized per service.

quiz.question: A scientific team wants to run a 32-core CPU-bound pipeline in one CPython process with threads. What do you change in the architecture?
quiz.optionA: Increase thread count to 256.
quiz.optionB: Use processes, a native GIL-releasing library, or another runtime; threads will not use the cores for bytecode.
quiz.optionC: Enable asyncio; it bypasses the GIL for CPU.
quiz.optionD: The GIL is gone for CPU loops if you `await` them.

quiz.question: You must ship a tool to air-gapped machines. What packaging failure mode should you design against?
quiz.optionA: wheels always contain every manylinux ABI.
quiz.optionB: Native deps, implicit system libraries, and 'pip install from PyPI' at runtime; vendoring/lock a compatible wheel set or use a frozen runtime.
quiz.optionC: CPython binaries are identical across distros.
quiz.optionD: venv is guaranteed present on all OS images.

quiz.question: A web worker pool + a background thread that mutates a dict without locks. GIL makes this 'safe', right?
quiz.optionA: Yes; GIL serializes all bytecode so dicts are atomic for any compound update.
quiz.optionB: No; GIL can interleave bytecode between operations; dict compound updates still need locks or a queue to a single owner thread.
quiz.optionC: dicts are immutable in CPython.
quiz.optionD: Only list.append needs a lock.

quiz.question: An ABI-stable plugin interface returns `std::string` across a `.so` boundary compiled with different libstdc++. What did you just do?
quiz.optionA: The Itanium ABI makes all std::string layouts identical forever.
quiz.optionB: You invoked ODR/ABI roulette: layout and allocators may differ; use a C ABI (char* + length) or a single shared standard library.
quiz.optionC: unique_ptr across .so is always safe if string is not.
quiz.optionD: C++ modules fix ABI at the filesystem boundary.

quiz.question: A low-latency path allocates on every message (std::string, vector resize). The profiler is 'clean' of locks. What is still wrong?
quiz.optionA: Allocators are wait-free and never stall.
quiz.optionB: Allocator contention and cache pollution; pre-size, arenas, or intrusive buffers belong on that path.
quiz.optionC: The compiler elides all heap use in loops.
quiz.optionD: virtual functions are the only latency bug that matters.

quiz.question: You need to share read-mostly config across threads. A shared_ptr swapped atomically vs a mutex around a unique_ptr. What is the RCU-like idea?
quiz.optionA: Mutex is always lower latency for reads.
quiz.optionB: Publish a new immutable snapshot (atomic shared_ptr); readers copy the pointer with no lock; old snapshot frees when refcount hits 0.
quiz.optionC: unique_ptr can be read from two threads if it is const.
quiz.optionD: atomics on unique_ptr are in the standard and cheaper.

quiz.question: A rate limiter for a global API: token bucket in one Redis vs sliding log of timestamps per user. What is the staff trade-off?
quiz.optionA: They are identical at all scales.
quiz.optionB: Token bucket is O(1) memory/CPU and approximate; a precise sliding log is memory-heavy per key and harder to shard. Pick based on fairness vs cost.
quiz.optionC: Sliding log is O(1) and token bucket is O(n).
quiz.optionD: Only a bloom filter can rate-limit correctly.

quiz.question: Autocomplete at 50k QPS: trie in one JVM vs prefix query to a search engine. When is the trie the wrong 'clever' answer?
quiz.optionA: Tries are always smaller than inverted indexes.
quiz.optionB: When the dictionary is huge, needs fuzzy/ranked results, or must be updated without STW rebuilds — operational cost dominates Big-O.
quiz.optionC: Search engines cannot do prefix match.
quiz.optionD: A trie cannot be sharded.

quiz.question: You need connectivity across a huge undirected graph that mutates. Why might union-find (DSU) be the right first tool, and when does it stop?
quiz.optionA: DSU supports deletions as cheaply as unions.
quiz.optionB: Near-constant unions/finds for 'are these connected' if you mostly add edges; deletions, path queries, or need for actual paths need a different structure.
quiz.optionC: DSU is only for trees of height 2.
quiz.optionD: BFS from every node is always faster.

quiz.question: A company wants to fine-tune on PII support tickets to 'make the model remember customers'. What should you block?
quiz.optionA: Fine-tuning cannot memorize.
quiz.optionB: Weights can memorize; you turned the model into a PII store that is hard to delete. Prefer RAG with access control over the tickets.
quiz.optionC: PII in prompts is fine if temperature is 0.
quiz.optionD: Fine-tunes automatically forget after 30 days.

quiz.question: You must ship a RAG system with a recall SLO. Embeddings-only search fails on SKUs and error codes. What do you add and why?
quiz.optionA: A larger embedding dimension always fixes exact tokens.
quiz.optionB: Hybrid retrieval (lexical + vector) because embeddings are weak on rare identifiers; keyword/BM25 still wins there.
quiz.optionC: Lower temperature.
quiz.optionD: Disable chunking so the embedding sees the whole corpus at once.

quiz.question: Offline eval is green; online users still jailbreak a tool-using assistant. What eval gap is this?
quiz.optionA: Offline eval cannot test tools.
quiz.optionB: You lacked adversarial/red-team cases and runtime policy on tools; capability eval ≠ security eval.
quiz.optionC: Jailbreaks only happen offline.
quiz.optionD: If BLEU is high, safety follows.

quiz.question: A 'fleet of agents' is proposed to run production deploys. What governance is non-negotiable?
quiz.optionA: More agents increase safety via debate.
quiz.optionB: Least-privilege tools, human approval gates on irreversible actions, full traces, and a non-agent rollback path.
quiz.optionC: If the planner is staff-level, tools can be root.
quiz.optionD: Traces are optional if the model is frontier.

quiz.question: You can give an agent a browser, a shell, and prod credentials 'so it can debug like a human'. Why is this a category error?
quiz.optionA: Agents cannot use browsers.
quiz.optionB: A human is accountable and rate-limited by attention; an agent will explore the union of permissions at machine speed. Split identities and environments.
quiz.optionC: Prod credentials are fine if in a vector store.
quiz.optionD: Debugging never needs write access, so the union is safe.

quiz.question: Multi-agent 'researcher + critic' improved a demo. In production it doubled cost and disagreed silently. What was missing?
quiz.optionA: A third agent.
quiz.optionB: A scoring contract, stop conditions, and a single owner of the user-visible answer; debate without a reducer is just extra tokens.
quiz.optionC: Critics should have more tools than researchers.
quiz.optionD: You should hide disagreements from traces.

flashcards.question: Why is a sync standby on the commit path a product decision?
flashcards.answer: Every COMMIT waits for that standby to flush WAL. You improved RPO and imported its availability and AZ latency into the primary's write SLO. If the standby flaps, writes stall. That can be correct for money; it is wrong for a best-effort cache.

flashcards.question: What breaks in transaction-pooling PgBouncer?
flashcards.answer: Anything that assumes a session lasts beyond one transaction: temp tables, SET, WITH HOLD cursors, session advisory locks, some prepared statement modes. Design the app for transaction pooling or use session pooling for the sessions that need it.

flashcards.question: How do you scale InnoDB writes when one primary is CPU-bound?
flashcards.answer: Reads can go to replicas; writes cannot. You shard the write key across primaries (or move that workload). One clustered B-tree will not become a write-horizontal system by adding replicas.

flashcards.question: Why can row-based replication still lag on bulk loads?
flashcards.answer: The primary may bulk-insert efficiently while the replica applies a huge stream of row events, often single-threaded per schema in older setups. Batching, parallel apply, and not using the replica as a synchronous read-your-writes node are the usual responses.

flashcards.question: Why isn't 'RocksDB + S3' a database?
flashcards.answer: You have a very good local engine. You still need replication, membership, fencing, and a commit protocol. Object storage is a persistence target, not consensus. People who skip this invent split brain.

flashcards.question: How do LSM tombstones become an outage?
flashcards.answer: Deletes are data until compaction drops them. If TTL/delete volume outruns compaction, reads scan graves and disk fills. Time-window compaction and bounded tombstone lifetimes are workload-specific, not defaults you ignore.

flashcards.question: What does LOCAL_QUORUM actually promise?
flashcards.answer: A quorum in the local DC, not a global latest. Other DCs can be behind until repair or replication catches up. Users who fail over DC without a consistency story will see time go backwards.

flashcards.question: Why is global uniqueness a Cassandra anti-pattern at scale?
flashcards.answer: Enforcing 'only one of this email' needs consensus on that key. LWT does it with Paxos per partition, which is slow and hot. A database with a unique index, or an allocation service, is usually the honest design.

flashcards.question: Why don't request-path joins belong in DynamoDB?
flashcards.answer: There are no server-side joins. You issue multiple queries, assemble a non-snapshot, and often add GSIs that create new hot keys. Duplicate data per access pattern or use a join-capable store.

flashcards.question: What still limits on-demand during a hot-key event?
flashcards.answer: On-demand removes most capacity planning, not physics. One partition key has a throughput ceiling. Famous items need caching, write sharding, or isolation.

flashcards.question: What makes a Redis lock correct enough to mutate a resource?
flashcards.answer: Expiry so it cannot live forever, and a fencing token so work started under an expired lock cannot still commit. SET NX without both is a mutex-shaped race.

flashcards.question: What is the RPO of async replica promotion?
flashcards.answer: Whatever was not replicated. Session stores and queues that only lived on the old primary are gone. If that RPO is unacceptable, wait for replication (costing latency) or store the source of truth elsewhere.

flashcards.question: Why do data lakes need a commit protocol?
flashcards.answer: S3 does not atomically swap a directory of files. Readers listing a prefix can see a mix of old and new. Iceberg/Delta/Hudi or a manifest file is the transaction log the object store does not provide.

flashcards.question: How do you debug a denied S3 request?
flashcards.answer: Identity policy, bucket policy, ACLs (legacy), SCP, and VPC endpoint policy all have to allow. A deny anywhere wins. 'The bucket policy looks open' is not a diagnosis.

flashcards.question: What happens when etcd is too big or too hot?
flashcards.answer: The API server is a strongly consistent bottleneck. Slow etcd means slow watches, delayed pod status, and scary control-plane elections. Treat object size/count as a budget; don't store blobs in annotations.

flashcards.question: Why must admission enforce requests on dedicated nodes?
flashcards.answer: A taint/selector without requests still lets BestEffort pods schedule there and get OOM-killed or eat CPU. Multi-tenant isolation is a policy you enforce, not a wiki page.

flashcards.question: When are GC flags not the answer?
flashcards.answer: When the live set is huge because the heap is a cache. You will pay pauses or RAM. Split instances, move cache off-heap or to Redis, and size heaps to the working set you can collect.

flashcards.question: Where should graceful shutdown live?
flashcards.answer: In the framework lifecycle and preStop, with a timeout less than terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Shutdown hooks racing SIGKILL are how you drop in-flight work.

flashcards.question: What is the outbox pattern doing in a Spring service?
flashcards.answer: You commit the business row and an 'event to send' in the same database transaction. A relay publishes after commit. Crashes retry the publish. You do not call Stripe inside the DB transaction and hope.

flashcards.question: Why is a shared database between services a distributed monolith?
flashcards.answer: Schema changes, locks, and entity meaning now require coordinated deploys. You lost independent release. Split ownership or accept you are one app in two repos.

flashcards.question: How do you use many cores from CPython?
flashcards.answer: Processes, or native code that releases the GIL (numpy, a Rust extension). Threads and asyncio overlap I/O; they do not parallelize bytecode. Architect the pipeline around that fact.

flashcards.question: Is the GIL a mutex for your dict?
flashcards.answer: No. It protects CPython internals, not your compound invariants. Two bytecode instructions can interleave around dict[k] += 1. Use a lock or a single-thread owner.

flashcards.question: Why is a C ABI the default plugin boundary?
flashcards.answer: std::string, exceptions, and STL layouts change across compilers and library versions. A C API (buffers, error codes) is stable. You can wrap it in C++ on each side.

flashcards.question: How do you publish read-mostly config to many threads?
flashcards.answer: Immutable snapshot + atomic shared_ptr (RCU-style): writers allocate a new object and swap the pointer; readers load the pointer and use it without a mutex. Old snapshots free when the last reader drops.

flashcards.question: Token bucket vs sliding log for rate limits?
flashcards.answer: Token bucket: constant memory, cheap, slightly bursty. Sliding window log: closer to 'N per real second', stores many timestamps, shards poorly. Most global limiters pick an approximate bucket and enforce it at the edge.

flashcards.question: When is a trie the wrong autocomplete?
flashcards.answer: When you need ranking, typos, freshness, and a dictionary that updates without rebuilding a giant heap object. An inverted index with prefix/edge n-grams is operationally boring and wins.

flashcards.question: Why not fine-tune on support tickets containing PII?
flashcards.answer: Training data can be extracted from weights. Deletion becomes 'retrain the model'. RAG over an access-controlled store lets you delete a ticket and it is gone.

flashcards.question: Why hybrid search for SKUs and error codes?
flashcards.answer: Dense embeddings smear rare tokens. BM25/keyword still finds `ECONNRESET` and `SKU-9F3`. Combine scores; don't expect vectors to be a primary key lookup.

flashcards.question: What is non-negotiable for an agent that can change prod?
flashcards.answer: Scoped credentials, allowlisted tools, human approval on irreversible steps, traces you can audit, and a rollback path that does not need the agent. Treat it as an untrusted intern with a terminal.

flashcards.question: What makes multi-agent debate fail in production?
flashcards.answer: Cost without a reducer. If two agents disagree, something must pick, score, or escalate. Otherwise you paid 2× tokens for a random winner. Define the contract before adding a critic.
